# GazeControl — Progress Board

Working memory for GazeControl (data-driven gaze control for virtual agents in a
triad conversation: two virtual agents + the user; gaze patterns collected before
turn-taking in real triad conversations drive the agents' gaze).

**Source of truth: this file.** `progress.html` is auto-generated from it on every
commit by the `progress-board` skill's pre-commit hook — never hand-edit the HTML.

Status legend: `[ ]` todo · `[~]` in progress · `[x]` done · `[!]` blocked.
Completed tasks carry a `_(done YYYY-MM-DD · <short-commit>)_` tag (the commit that
finished them, for history tracking); the dashboard keeps full detail for the most
recent few completed items and compacts older ones.

  - [x] **Mouth interior fixed properly (real mouth-bag geometry)** — the body FBX was replaced with a Blender re-export that carries an actual mouth bag, and that geometry is split onto its own submesh with a dark material at import time. Retires the `MouthCavity`/`MouthBackdrop` blockers entirely: they are deleted from the scene, along with `MouthCavityTools.cs` and `MouthCavity.mat` _(done 2026-08-02)_
    - **The bag carries no UV mapping.** All 161 of its vertices (129 new ones plus the inner-lip rim that was merged into them) collapse onto UV (0, 0), so the whole cavity samples a single texel — the bottom-left corner of whichever albedo the agent wears. That corner is RGB(77, 85, 84) in the stock 4096² SMPL-X atlas (reads black) but RGB(245, 246, 241) in the 512² SMPLitex one, which is exactly why Agent A looked right and Agent B looked grey. Nothing else uses that texel: the nearest mapped UV is 0.029 away (15 px at 512², 120 px at 4096²).
    - `SmplxMouthInteriorSubmesh` (an `AssetPostprocessor`) moves every triangle whose three vertices all sit on UV (0, 0) — exactly 288 of the mesh's 21196 — onto submesh 1 and assigns `SMPLX-MouthInterior.mat` (URP Lit, base colour 0.055/0.02/0.02). There are no partially-mapped seam triangles, so the rule has no edge cases. Idempotent across reimports, and the scene needed no overrides: the second material slot is inherited from the model prefab.
    - **The FBX swap was a true drop-in.** Same node names (plus 15 unbound `*_end` leaf bones from Blender), same single source material, and the 520 blendshapes identical in name and order — so visemes stay at 506-519. Overwriting the asset in place kept its GUID, and both agents kept their materials, bone bindings and lipsync morph targets. Source vertices went 10475 → 10604; the file roughly doubled to 58 MB in LFS.
    - Chosen over a Blender-side material split (a round trip per model revision) and over painting the texture corner dark (needs redoing for every new agent texture). Blocker-era tuning notes are dropped with the approach; the one durable gotcha — that renders in the *same* editor command as a state change show stale geometry — is already in `CLAUDE.md`.

    - **The manual eye-disc composite is now a menu item**, `GazeControl → Textures → Composite SMPLitex Eye Disc`. SMPLitex never generates the eyeball island and leaves it black; both eyes share it, so an untreated texture gives black eyes. Pixels are read from the PNG rather than the imported texture, which is DXT1 — round-tripping through block compression to fix one disc would degrade the whole image. The (296, 221) r≈19 geometry from the 2026-07-26 note is **top-left origin**, confirmed by finding pure black there in the new textures and the composited disc there in the old one.
    - **`Pad SMPLitex UV Islands`** fills the gaps between islands from their edges, with the mesh's own UVs as the coverage mask, so nothing a triangle covers is ever written. It also repairs a flat background spilled *into* an island — but only when the background is measurably flat, which is checked rather than assumed (the modal outside-island colour must hold ≥50% of outside texels). It manages the FBX's Read/Write flag itself instead of leaving the project carrying it.
    - **Not fixed, and it was in the source:** `smplitex_f00016_alb.png` had yellow-green painted on the fingers and toes *inside* the islands. Three attempts to remove it failed on the same fact — there is no flat background to subtract. The modal outside-island colour is black at only **11.9%**, and the next seven (greys and pinks) each occur in 15k-43k *island* texels, so any colour rule that caught the green would eat real content. Reported rather than hand-tuned away; swapping the SMPLitex sample was named as the clean fix, and that is what happened below.

  - [x] **Every EoT event draws its own prototype, matched to its class** — the fifteen prototypes the paper prints are all transcribed now, pooled by class (5 interruption / 4 overlapping / 6 turn-taking), and each boundary draws from the pool for *its* class _(done 2026-08-10)_
    - `Tools/build_gaze_patterns.py` generates `GazePatterns.g.cs` from the raw archives. Decoding: kernel column = role track (current speaker / next speaker / listener), value = gaze target (0 aversion, 1 current speaker, 2 next speaker, 3 listener). The generator **asserts Fig7e and Fig8d still decode to the two hand transcriptions** the earlier demos were signed off on, so a decoding change cannot silently rewrite a signed-off take.
    - Listener tracks are transcribed but never rendered — the listener is the human user. Gaze *at* the listener is rendered, and several prototypes call for it.
    - The draw is `FNV-1a(BaseSeed, eventIndex)`, **not** the per-agent seed: both agents must play tracks of the same prototype or they would play two different patterns at each other. It is also independent of tick count, so it survives a change of decision rate. The whole mapping is computed up front and written into the log's metadata sidecar.

  - [ ] **BUG: case-1 takes start and end mid-sentence** — the user hears the audio "cut" (asked 2026-08-16 whether backchannels had been removed). **They have not been**, and nothing is lost anywhere in the pipeline — the cut is the *window*, not the audio
    - **Ruled out, with measurements.** The export is a verbatim contiguous trim: `case1_seg02/03/04` re-derive from the corpus **sample-exact** (max diff 1, pure rounding). The recorded takes contain that audio complete — envelope correlation **0.9998-1.0000** at a constant 0.20 s scheduling offset, **zero** dropped bins at 50 ms resolution. A/V stream lengths agree to ≤17 ms in every take. `load_utterances` explicitly keeps backchannels, with a comment saying why.
    - **Root cause:** `PAUSE_THRESHOLD = 0.3` s. The selection rule only forbids a boundary *inside* a pause-delimited run of words, so any 0.3 s breath counts as a legal place to cut. `case1_seg02` opens on "subscription forever." (the speaker had said "I will just have my." just before) and closes on "They do not get a lot of"; `case1_seg04` closes on "Let us see, the one that adores her is". Sentence-final punctuation is right there in the word-level TSV and simply is not consulted.
    - **Fix is cheap and the corpus affords it:** require the window to open just after a sentence-final token and close on one — the same `[.?!]` test scene 2 already uses for its question tier. Measured over all 186 conversations: **737 of 1,807 windows (40.8%)** have both edges sentence-clean, so the ranking keeps plenty to choose from. Needs a re-export and re-record of the case-1 takes.
  - [x] **Exported segment audio is peak-normalised, and baseline B was silently broken without it** — the corpus records at about **−42 dBFS**, so no frame ever reached the VAD's 0.01 RMS threshold and both agents sat on their fallback target (the user) for the entire take _(done 2026-08-10)_
    - Caught by the user watching the first takes and asking why the agents never look at each other. The gaze logs answered it immediately: **100% of baseline B's frames targeted the user**, which is precisely what "nobody is ever detected as speaking" looks like.
    - The exporter now peak-normalises to 0.70 with **one gain for both sides**, taken from the louder track (51.3× here). Per-track normalisation would rewrite the balance between the two speakers, which is recorded rather than incidental. Gain and pre-gain peak go into `segment.json`.
    - Checked the tracks really are speaker-separated before touching levels: during their own speaker's words each track carries **8-16× the energy** it does during the other's, and the two envelopes are anti-correlated (−0.16). Against the transcript, the normalised audio at the 0.01 threshold detects **86-89% of speech frames with 9-11% false positives on silence** — which is what the tracker's hysteresis exists to clean up.
  - [x] **Baseline B: two §3 conformance gaps that only real audio could expose** — with corpus audio the VAD and the turn schedule genuinely disagree, and each disagreement produced an agent gazing at itself (5% of A's frames, 16% of B's) _(done 2026-08-10)_
    - **`current_addressee` belongs to whoever holds the floor**, so when an agent speaks off-schedule the field names that agent itself. An agent is not its own addressee; §3's own fallback clause now covers it.
    - **Backchannel suppression was applied only to partners, never to self.** §3 says utterances under 600 ms trigger no gaze switch; the self-speaking branch ignored that, so every "yeah" re-aimed the agent. Now applied uniformly.

At 250/role the worst cell sat 0.08 off the corpus S (the occupancy test asserts 0.06); at 500/role it is 0.028 with all nine cells inside. The full pool reproduces S to 4 decimals, so this is pure sampling variance, measured before choosing the size.
    - **Replay quantises each fixation to its nearest tick count** (advance when < half a tick remains), not baseline A's `<= 0` dwell test: recorded durations are exact (0.5 s = 15 ticks at 30 Hz) and accumulated float error at the boundary otherwise adds a 16th tick — caught by four tests at once.
    - **Comparison set refreshed 2026-08-14**: new Proposed takes `case1_seg02_02` / `case1_seg03_02` / `case1_seg04_02`, each frame-identical in length to its case's old set, with the user drawing 4-50% of out-of-window gaze and aversion 20-53% depending on who holds the floor. The old Proposed videos in the `_01` folders are **not stale — they are valid ablation takes**: what they recorded (baseline B substrate + prototypes) is bit-for-bit today's `Substrate = SpeakerFollowing` configuration, and their sidecars already say so. Baseline A/B videos in the `_01` folders stay valid (those conditions are untouched). The scene now serializes `Substrate` explicitly and is left on `CaseName = case1_seg02_03` so a stray Record Demo lands in a fresh folder.
    - Refactor pass done (four-angle review): `Emit` is now a pure projection with the self-gaze rule hoisted into `Update`; the derivable `_target`/`_averting`/`RoleOfTarget` state is gone; the 525 KB TextAsset is unloaded after parsing. Deliberately skipped: sharing the role-assignment block and corpus key maps with baseline A (would touch the verified `ShintaniGazePolicy`/`ShintaniGazeParameters` for zero behavioural gain; the mirroring is the sibling-policy convention), and cross-fixture test-helper extraction (fixtures define their own builders by convention).
    - **Verified end to end and signed off by the user 2026-08-14.** Test take `case1_seg02_02`: outside the windows agent B looks at the user 50% / agent A 4% (0% before the change) and both avert with recentred eyes (40% / 20%, all offsets zero); the windows play the same Fig6d/Fig7e prototypes as the signed-off takes; sidecar carries `"substrate": "HoldingReplay"` and the bank provenance. User watched the video and called it natural.
  - [ ] **Replay harness (§7.6)** — re-run a logged transcript through any policy offline, so objective metrics need no participants
  - The runner logs forever once started; it should end the session when the conversation finishes. Harmless for a recorded take (the recorder exits Play Mode, so the 11.7 s takes give ~80 KB logs), but a free-running session still grows without bound.
- [~] **3People-2022 mocap → SMPL-X converter** — a tool turning the three-party conversation capture (Vicon joint-angle export) into SMPL-X `.npz` clips this project can play
  - [x] **Source directories surveyed and documented** — `Assets/Docs/3people-motion-sources.md` records the three roots (`{TPC_CODE}` = `F:\Code\Multi-TPC`, `{TPC_DATA}` = `D:\3People-2022`, `{TPC_VIEWER}` = `F:\Code\Conversation_Demo`), their file structure, the motion file schema and the conventions the reference C++ viewer establishes _(done 2026-09-07)_
    - **69 participant-sessions** (7 dates, 23 sessions × 3 participants) at 60 fps. Input is `mocap/<date>/Mocap/Separate/Session_<S>_PC_<N>_mocap_data.txt`: 66 space-separated floats — 19 joints × 3 Euler degrees, then 3 translation triplets.
    - **The three translation triplets are different kinds of quantity**, measured rather than assumed: `pelvis<t-*>` is a global room position (z ≈ 917 mm), while `thorax<t-*>` (‖·‖ ≈ 120 mm) and `head<t-*>` (‖·‖ ≈ 335 mm) are **constant local bone offsets** with ~4 mm s.d. over a whole session. Torso segment lengths are therefore measurable per participant; limb lengths are absent from the export but present in the Vicon VSKs (see `{TPC_VICON}` below).
    - Source rest pose is **arms-down (I-pose)**, confirmed twice over: `Figures/skeleton.png` shows it, and the viewer's ∓90°-about-Z pre-rotation of the Mixamo upper arms is exactly the T-pose→arms-down correction.
  - [ ] **Decide the joint-splitting and rest-alignment conventions** — the source has 19 joints against SMPL-X's 55: `thorax` must spread over `spine1/2/3` and `head` over `neck`+`head` (any split preserving the total keeps global head orientation, which is what the gaze work needs), fingers/jaw/eyes stay zero (jaw and eyes are driven at runtime by LipSync and `IGazePolicy`, so they must not be baked)
  - [ ] **Converter + validation** (angle-retargeting route) — write the `.npz` (`poses` (F,165) axis-angle, `trans` (F,3) m, `mocap_frame_rate`), right-handed Y-up as `SmplxAnimUtils` expects
    - **A quantitative oracle already exists**: `Session_<S>_gazeBehavior.txt` is a pure function of the three head poses (`Data/main.cpp` ray-casts eye rays at head spheres), so re-running that test against converted SMPL-X heads should reproduce the committed annotation. Plus side-by-side against `{TPC_VIEWER}`, which renders the same take from the same file.
  - [x] **Original Vicon project located and surveyed** — `{TPC_VICON}` = `D:People-2024Party-Conversation-2022` (pointed out by the user 2026-09-07), upstream of everything in `{TPC_DATA}/mocap` and **it changes the answer**: 70 C3D files of 41-marker Plug-in Gait data at 60 Hz plus 28 per-participant `.vsk` skeleton templates _(done 2026-09-07)_
    - **The VSK settles by construction what had to be inferred from the viewer**: the 19-segment hierarchy in export column order; the joint types, whose DOF explain **all fourteen always-zero export columns** exactly (hinges write one axis, Hardy-Spicers two, each into the slot matching its axis); and the rest pose numerically — `EDIT_POSE_MEAN` is `±1.5708 0 0` on the humeri, which is the ∓90° arm rotation the viewer hardcodes. Also **per-participant anthropometrics** (Thigh, Shin, UpperArm, LowerArm, Back, Neck…) for all 28 subject-days, so limb proportions are recoverable after all. `12-10-2021/Feyza.vsk` is an unfitted default (every value a round number).
    - **The user's warning about markers is right and now quantified**: 62 of 70 files carry the full 41; eight are short by one or two, consistently per subject (Maryum `T10`/`RHEE`, May `T10`, Clayton `LANK`, Elian `RSHO`, Ahmed `RTHI`). Within a file there are **no gaps** — every declared marker is valid in every frame sampled. Two traps: `3-4-2022/Convo002.c3d` is the un-split 246-point original, and `2-11-2022/convo3_pc*.c3d` report 65535 frames because the 16-bit header field saturates (true length **69,507**).
    - **Markers and the export share a room frame and a clock**: same Z-up mm coordinates, and the export's `Frame` column is the C3D frame index (`Session_<S>` ↔ `convo<S>`, each range sitting inside its take with margin). Two dates have VSKs but no C3D (12-10-2021, 4-1-2022); 4-1-2022 has no processed counterpart at all.
    - **This opens a second route for the converter**: fit SMPL-X to the markers (MoSh-style, shape *and* pose) instead of retargeting Euler angles — which removes the Euler ambiguity outright and recovers per-participant body shape rather than posing a default body. Angle retargeting is still the fast path to something on screen. **Route not yet chosen.**
  - Rigid hands and an unarticulated neck are properties of the capture and will be visible next to the TalkingWithHands agents (the marker set has one finger marker per hand — enough for wrist orientation, not articulated fingers).

## Decisions

- 2026-09-07 — **Angle retargeting is the first route for the 3People-2022 converter; marker fitting is deferred, not dropped** (user's call). The processed export's Euler angles get retargeted onto SMPL-X, accepting the Euler-order risk and a default body, because it is the fast path to something on screen. The alternative — a MoSh-style fit of SMPL-X shape *and* pose to `{TPC_VICON}`'s 41-marker C3D — removes the Euler ambiguity outright and recovers per-participant body shape, and stays the better answer if fidelity ever outranks turnaround.
  - **The two routes share the joint map, the rest-pose alignment problem and the validation oracle**, so the second is an upgrade of the first rather than a rewrite. Build accordingly: keep the Euler order behind one named constant so switching it is a single edit, and use the VSK even on this route — `EDIT_POSE_MEAN` gives the arms-down rest pose numerically and the per-participant segment lengths give a real root scale instead of a guessed one.
- 2026-09-07 — **`Notes.xlsx` is the participant register, and it exposes a labelling defect in the processed motion.** Each `mocap/<date>/Notes.xlsx` names the machines outright (`PC 1 (Crystal)`, `PC 2 (Maryum)`, `PC 3 (Justice)`) and carries the per-stream sync data besides — per-PC audio/visual start/stop in UTC epoch ms, total frames, an offset in frames against the mocap, and the mocap's own `Start`/`Stop`/`Total` (951 / 37249 / 36298 for 12-15-2021 S1, exactly the range measured in the export). **So stream alignment never has to be estimated.** Set against it, `Separate/..._PC_<N>_...` numbers participants by alphabetical position instead, and is wrong in 16 of 21 slots. See the open question for the consequences.
- 2026-09-07 — **The 3People-2022 Euler order is a decision, not a discovery: adopt `Data/main.cpp`'s XYZ.** The two reference readers in `{TPC_VIEWER}` disagree and neither documents itself. In the file's own axes, `Data/main.cpp` composes `Rx(aX)·Ry(aY)·Rz(aZ)` (**XYZ**) via an explicit `glm::rotate` sequence, while `Demo/main.cpp` — the renderer — composes `Rx(aX)·Rz(aZ)·Ry(aY)` (**XZY**) through `glm::quat(vec3(y, z, x))`, whose constructor was read in the vendored `glm/detail/type_quat.inl:204-213` rather than recalled. They agree only to second order in the two smaller angles; on a real pelvis row the quaternions differ by ≈ 5°.
  - **The data cannot settle it and that was tested, not assumed.** Only three joints carry translations and two of those turned out to be constant bone offsets, so there is no positional redundancy to check rotations against; a search over all six orders left the candidates within 0.5 mm of each other. **The VSKs found later the same day do not settle it either** — the model stores ball/free joints as axis-angle, so the Euler order belongs to Vicon's exporter rather than to the model.
  - XYZ wins because it is what produced the published `Session_<S>_gazeBehavior.txt` annotations that the dataset's own analysis rests on — agreeing with the corpus of record beats being independently "right".
  - **A better answer now exists: bypass the decision.** `{TPC_VICON}`'s C3D markers let joint orientations be computed from marker triads — or SMPL-X fitted to the markers directly — with no Euler decoding anywhere. Prefer that if the converter is built properly; XYZ stands only as the fallback for the angle-retargeting route.
  - **The head is where this matters most**, which is unlucky for this project: it carries the largest secondary angles in the data (aY to ±21°, aZ to ±38°), so it is exactly the joint the two conventions disagree about worst. Worth re-testing against the gaze-behaviour oracle once the converter runs.
- 2026-09-05 — **The study is done, and it split.** 18 participants (P05-P22), all 15 clips each. **H_inc is verified and is the strongest result in the project**: our method and baseline A both sit more than two scale points above baseline B on "the characters seemed aware I was there" (2.51 points, 95% CI [2.12, 2.90], *d_z* = 1.69), 16 of 18 participants in the predicted direction with **none against**, and the effect reproduces in all five conversations. **H_bnd is verified against baseline B only** (0.78 points, Holm *p* < .001 under the registered model; *p* = .036 with a random method slope; *p* = .074 on participant means — all three are reported). **H_nat and H_rank failed to reject the null**, which are exactly the contrasts the registration had pre-committed to reading as inconclusive. **H_eng is not verified**: baseline B beat baseline A, our method did not.
  - **Why the primary measure did not separate, and it is not a shrug.** Refitting each construct with a random method slope by participant puts nearly all of the participant-by-method variance on **baseline B**: its component runs 1.11-1.88 across the four constructs against 0.01-0.26 for baseline A. Participants agreed with one another about both stochastic policies and split sharply over the deterministic one, which took first place in 26 blocks and last in 41. A forced ranking of three cannot separate a field in which one competitor is polarizing rather than uniformly weak.
  - **The free responses name the ceiling.** Four participants complained about the *head* rather than the eyes ("head is not turning with gaze", "eye moves without head movement"), which is the shared animation layer and identical in all three conditions by construction. That is the standing explanation for the naturalness null, and it is the limitation section 6 already predicted before the data existed.
  - **The discriminant check passed.** Our method did not beat baseline B on mutual engagement — the pattern a halo or a demand effect cannot produce — so the wins that did land read as real rather than as compliance.
  - **What the paper may therefore claim**: the vocabulary is perceived where it acts, at turn boundaries, and it makes agents read as aware of a co-present third party. It may **not** claim demonstrated naturalness, and the abstract and contributions must be pitched to that.
  - **Three participants found being looked at unwelcome** ("like the user should not be there"). Inclusion and comfort are not the same axis, and I1 measures only the first — worth a sentence in the Discussion.

- 2026-09-02 (later still) — **Both question pages are previewed before the first clip, and the short-answer page carries a `Next: group x` foot.** Showing the six questions once up front is cheap (one screen, one key) and changes what the participant does with the first group: they watch it knowing they will rate four things about each version and then rank the three, rather than meeting those questions after the last version has played. The foot is the only progress indicator in the study — five groups is long enough that not knowing where you are is its own fatigue — and it is absent after the last group, where the closing passage is what follows.

- 2026-09-02 (later) — **The ranking and the free-text probe are one page for the participant, titled `Short Answer` and numbered 5 and 6**, continuing the four rating items, and the "say your answer out loud" footnote is deleted from every page. The page carries the prompts alone. Six numbered questions per conversation is one instrument to read rather than four numbered ones and two loose prompts; the footnote was on every page and told the participant what the operator tells them anyway. The entry side is unchanged — the operator still commits the ranks and the comment separately.

- 2026-09-02 — **The participant's rating screen shows the answers back.** It is headed `Rating`, numbers the four items and gives each a box that fills with the number the operator typed — the operator panel's own layout, on the participant's side. This reverses 2026-08-27's "never show an answer back" (whose worry was priming the next answer with the last one), because the larger risk in answering aloud is the answer being heard or typed wrong with nobody able to see it. The `>` still marks the item being asked, and the ranking screen still lists nothing.

- 2026-09-01 — **The pre-roll shows neutral eyes; the opening second of a take stays exactly as baked.** A participant reported being looked at on the first frame. The half that is ours to choose — the gaze held while a segment loads and the voices are scheduled, before any policy has decided anything — is now recentred eyes rather than the human participant, because it is a gaze state no condition was baked to produce and it primed "the character noticed me" before the clip existed. The half that is inside the fifteen baked tracks is left alone: re-baking to remove it would make P05 onwards incomparable, which costs more than the artifact does. It is now a stated limitation rather than an unnoticed one.

- 2026-09-01 (later) — **Data exposure matches ISMAR 2024: nothing from the participant side is released.** That paper publishes its training corpus, its model/code and its instrument, and not one participant-level file — no responses, no eye-tracking logs, no video (`Research/notes/ismar2024-agent-behavior-generation-user-study.md` §11). We do the same, so `Recordings/` stays out (it is already git-ignored) and the paper makes no data-availability claim.
  - **What we can expose that they could not**, at no privacy cost: the stimulus is deterministic recorded playback, so segment definitions, baked 60 Hz tracks and seeds reconstruct every trial frame for frame without containing a participant. Their stimulus was a live LLM conversation and was unreproducible by construction.
  - **Consequence for the registration**: with no data released, its commit timestamp is not externally checkable and its value is internal — it stops the analysis drifting. Its header now states the real sequence (written 2026-08-31 before P05; committed 2026-09-01 after P05-P07) rather than claiming the commit preceded collection.
  - **What has and has not been read of P05-P07**: their presentation order, yes — that is what verified the counterbalancing was in force and it is independent of their answers. Their responses, no. Recorded in `study-registration.md` §1 so the boundary is on the record rather than remembered.
  - **Do not copy ISMAR's missing ethics statement** — it has no IRB, consent or approval statement anywhere, which ISMAR tolerated and CHI reviewers would not.

- 2026-09-01 (latest) — **Starting a participant session is a window, not a checklist of inspector fields** (prompted by the user: no clear instruction for how to start a real recording, the participant ID edited by hand, mistakes easy). Three choices inside it:
  - **The participant label is derived from disk rather than typed or remembered.** `Alt+N` was the only thing between two participants and one filename, and forgetting it was silent — the guard caught `P00` and an empty label, never a repeat. The roster reads `Recordings/` and proposes one past the highest, so the operator confirms a number instead of authoring one, and a label whose folder exists is refused outright.
  - **One rule set, two readers.** The same pure rules answer the runner's `Awake` guard and the window's Edit-Mode preflight. Duplicating them is how a window comes to say ready for a run that `Awake` then refuses — with the participant already wearing the headset, which is the moment the whole thing exists to avoid.
  - **The launch is play-session state, not a scene edit.** Setting the six study fields in Edit Mode would leave the committed scene dirty in study state for the next bake or demo recording to inherit, and would need remembering to undo. A request in `SessionState`, applied by `StudySessionRunner.Awake`, has neither problem: the scene asset is never touched and there is nothing to put back.

- 2026-08-31 — **The analysis plan is registered, by commit, at N = 18 (P05-P22).** `Assets/Docs/study-registration.md` fixes the sample, exclusion rules, hypotheses, measures and tests before any analysed participant runs. **No external registry** (user's call), so the paper says the analysis was *fixed in advance and recorded in the project repository* and must never say "pre-registered" — readers take that to mean a third-party record with a citable identifier. The draft's previous "pre-registered" claim was false and is gone.
  - **What the registration is careful about**: it states up front that the four pilots' responses had already been inspected and that the power calculation derives from them, and it registers the *negative* — that N = 18 cannot resolve Proposed vs B on N1 and T2 (pilot *d_z* ≈ 0.5 against a sensitivity of 0.69), so those are reported as inconclusive rather than as null results. H_eng's predicted null on A1 is registered as a discriminant check: a Proposed > B result there counts against the instrument, not for the method.

- 2026-08-31 — **P01-P04 are pilots and are excluded; the analysed study starts at P05 under a per-participant counterbalanced schedule.** The four ran the single fixed method order of 2026-08-27, every one of them the same one, so a "balanced permutation" claim could not be made about a sample containing them. Rewriting their recorded `version_position` to fit a design they did not run was refused; excluding them makes the design sentence true instead of merely arguable. Declared before any further participant runs, on the ground of *how their session was ordered* — not on anything they answered — and the fact that their responses had already been inspected is disclosed in `user-study-design.md` §0.1 rather than left implicit.
  - **The counterbalancing is back at no cost to recoverability.** Block *b* of participant ordinal *i* takes permutation `(i + b) mod 6`. The 2026-08-27 fixed order was defending against a *runtime shuffle*, where a misnamed log cannot be placed; a **pre-generated** schedule is a pure function of the label, so the order is recovered by lookup. Within a participant the five blocks still take five different permutations (each method in each position once or twice); across any six consecutive participants every block sees all six, so the marginals close **exactly** — which is why the registered N = 18 is a multiple of six. Asserted at N = 6 and at N = 18 in `StudySequenceTest`.
  - **N = 20 was rejected as impossible to balance**: 20 × 5 = 100 block-orders over 9 method × position cells gives an ideal of 33.33, so no scheme closes at that N. 18 and 24 both do; 18 chosen.
  - **A take now places itself.** `block`, `version_position` and `schedule_ordinal` go into the take sidecar, named as `responses.csv` names them so the two join without translation. Written only on a session take — a bake or a preview omits them, so their presence is the signal that a take belongs to a participant's session. Before this the sidecar knew participant and condition but not position, which was harmless under one fixed order and stops being so now that the order varies by participant.

- 2026-08-31 — **Participant eye tracking is out of scope; objective evidence moves to the stimulus side.** §6.1 tells the participant to attend to the characters' eye movements and they can never take a turn, so a tracker records task-driven scanning under an instruction, not third-party gaze. Allocation would measure instruction compliance, mutual gaze is inflated identically in all conditions, and gaze-return latency is *floored* — someone already fixating faces has no return to make. The ISMAR-2024 comparison is the point: their participants conversed freely, so those measures mean what they say; ours would not.
  - **Confirmed empirically at zero cost**: across P01-P04 every one of ~97,500 logged ticks reads `tracker=Invalid, calibrated=0` — the tracker never delivered a sample in sixty clips. Head pose was captured and is real.
  - **What replaces it**: distributional fidelity of the generated gaze against `gaze_events_md6.csv` — role-conditioned target proportions, dwell distributions, shift timing around EoT events — computed over the baked tracks, needing no participants. It fits the thesis better than participant tracking did: *the gaze reproduces human statistics* and *people prefer it* are two halves of one argument.
  - The capture stays built and running (it costs nothing); nothing is promised as an analysis.

- 2026-08-31 — **Three stale claims in the draft's user-study section corrected against the code.** It still described the superseded per-participant counterbalancing *and* justified N = 30 by it; it claimed per-participant eye-height calibration, which the fixed 1.6846 m viewpoint replaced on 2026-08-27; and it had participants answering "in VR with a controller pointer", which the display-only canvas and spoken answers replaced the same day. Also **the decision grid is 60 Hz, not 30** — the sidecars say so and `baseline-spec.md` explains why (both sources are 60 fps; at 30 Hz every other fixation duration rounds, 8.17 ms mean error against 0.02 ms) — corrected in the draft and in `CLAUDE.md`.
  - **"The analysis is fixed before data collection and pre-registered" was false**: no registration exists anywhere, and collection began 2026-08-27. Reworded to what is true — fixed in the design document ahead of the analysed sample. Registering it properly before P05 is still open.

- 2026-08-28 — **State that describes the scene is sampled once, not re-sampled on every re-arm.** The one-scene/no-reload session means every `Initialize`-style method now runs fifteen times against a scene the previous clip has already moved, so anything read from the scene as a baseline has to be captured before the first clip or explicitly restored first. `SmplxMotionPlayer` re-read the pelvis rest pose and accumulated a metre of drift; `GazeController` had already met the same hazard on the head and guarded it. Treat re-arm as the default case when adding scene-derived state, not the exception.

- 2026-08-27 — **The questionnaire is shown in the headset after all, and it is built.** The user found in VR verification that nothing appeared after a clip; the cause was that only the data layer had ever been written. Restoring the in-VR canvas settles a contradiction the repo had been carrying since the morning — the decisions log had the items on a world-space canvas, `ClipPauseController`'s doc claimed a later call that they were answered outside VR — in favour of the logged design.
  - **The participant still points at nothing.** Display-only in the headset, spoken answers, operator entry on the desktop: that is what keeps XRI, ray interactors and an untested controller path under the Varjo loader out of the study.
  - **The operator panel stays blinded**, which is the reason to build entry as its own surface rather than reusing the developer overlay: the experimenter reads the items aloud, so naming the condition would tell them which answer is the interesting one.
  - The seam to the harness is two hold flags rather than a rewrite: a questionnaire screen holds the pause and the session start, and releases them when it is answered. Without a questionnaire in the scene the fifteen clips still walk on one key exactly as before.

- 2026-08-27 — **The agents' textures are decided by the clip, at segment load, not by the scene.** The voices were measured per clip from the start, but the pairing was only ever applied by hand from the Clip Browser, so a session showed one pair of bodies for all fifteen takes. Applying it in `RecordedConversation.TryLoadSegment` rather than in `StudySessionRunner` was deliberate: the session is not the only thing that loads a segment, and a fix that only covered the session would leave previews and bakes showing something the study does not.
  - Materials are resolved by project path in the editor rather than from serialized fields, following the segment's audio clips — the clip set changes as segments are re-exported, and per-material wired fields would have to be re-dragged each time. A build would need them wired in the scene.

- 2026-08-27 — **The fifteen clips run in one fixed order, the same for every participant** (user's call, superseding `user-study-design.md` §1's per-participant counterbalancing). The reason is operational rather than statistical: with one known order, a log that goes missing or arrives misnamed is still identifiable by the position it occupied.
  - **The confound this would have created is largely dissolved by balancing within the participant.** A single order shared by everyone makes serial position collinear with method — but only if the order is the same in every *block*. `StudySequence` picks the five permutations so each method sits in each serial position once or twice, which is as even as five blocks over three positions allows, so position effects average out within each participant. My first reading of the request was more alarmed than the request deserved.
  - **What is genuinely given up**, and is now written into §1 as a limitation: order effects no longer average across the sample as well as within it, and the N = 30 multiple-of-six argument no longer applies.
  - It also stops a participant learning that "the third one is always the proposed method", which back-to-back repetition would otherwise teach by block three.

- 2026-08-27 — **A session re-arms its components in place rather than reloading the scene between clips.** A reload was the safer-looking option — every component keeps its Awake-once contract, which is where the August reproducibility bug lived — but it would tear the headset down fifteen times and drop the participant out of the experience at every clip. Instead `GazeConditionRunner.Awake` is factored into `ArmTake()`, and `BeginTake()` calls the *same* method: a parallel "reset" path is precisely how a re-run comes to differ from a first run.
  - **The ordering constraint was found by the existing guards, not by reasoning.** `LoadSegment` → `BeginTake` → `PlayLoadedAsync`: the runner validates its baked track against the *loaded* segment's name, so the segment must be in place before it is armed; but it must be armed before the conversation's clock starts, since that clock anchors every decision grid. One `RestartAsync` could not satisfy both, and the track guard refused `study_c1`'s track against a still-loaded `study_c5` rather than playing the wrong take.
  - **Determinism across re-arms is argued, not measured.** Trial 1 of a session should be byte-identical to a fresh play of that clip. Given the August history that should be verified before real participants.

- 2026-08-27 — **One key (Space) starts the session, skips a clip, and advances past a pause**, so a whole pass can be walked in a minute while testing. **Skip is refused when `StudySession` is on**: the same key advances and skips, so a mistimed press would cut a participant's clip short and leave a take that looks complete and is not — the same class of quietly-worthless trial the switch already guards five other ways.
  - The agents are hidden while the participant answers. Correctness rather than presentation: the runner keeps ticking past the end of the conversation, so otherwise they would rate "seemed aware I was there" while two agents gazed at them in a state no condition was ever baked to produce.
  - A zero `tailSeconds` means "use the recorder's 1.5 s default", **not** "no hold" — every scene-1 segment carries zero, so reading it literally cut the agents away on the participant's last syllable. `ClipPauseController` mirrors `DemoRecorder`'s rule so a live session ends the way a recorded video of the same clip does.

- 2026-08-27 — **`P00` is reserved for debugging and a study session refuses to start on it** (user's call). Every development run this project has ever done writes `P00_…` files; a participant left on the default would file fifteen takes into that same namespace, separable only by timestamp and only if someone noticed. Real participants start at `P01`, one **Alt+N** away. Zero-padding is preserved rather than normalised (`P09` → `P10`, widening only at `P99`) so a 30-participant study keeps sorting in run order.
  - The shortcut is **Alt+N, not a bare key**, and it deliberately does *not* touch `GazeParticipant.Id`. A first attempt put an increment button on that field; the user removed it, correctly — triad ids are array indices, bit positions and seed inputs, and must never move by accident.

- 2026-08-27 — **The participant's initial orientation is recentred on the agents, and only in yaw** (user's request). The fixed viewpoint solved *where* the participant stands but not *which way they face*: the headset's yaw zero comes from the room's tracking setup, so a session could start with the triad off to one side or behind them, and every trial would differ by however the room was configured that day.
  - **Yaw only, and this is the load-bearing part.** Pitch and roll are reported against gravity and are therefore already correct; recentring them would tilt the virtual horizon away from the real one, which is both wrong and the most reliable way to make a participant ill. The yaw is read from the forward vector's horizontal projection rather than `eulerAngles.y`, which mixes roll into yaw well before the poles — a participant with a tilted head would otherwise be recentred wrong by tens of degrees.
  - **Refused rather than guessed near vertical.** Looking straight up leaves yaw undefined and near-vertical swings it on noise, so a head pitched more than ~80 degrees from level is rejected with a reason. The operator is standing there and can ask again; the alternative (deriving yaw from the head's up vector) trades a clear failure for a quiet wrong answer.
  - **Automatic, but bounded.** It cannot run inside `StartXr` because the runtime has no pose that early, so it retries until the first usable frame — and gives up after 15 s. Without the bound, a headset picked up ten minutes into a session would snap the view mid-take and quietly ruin the trial.
  - **"Centred" is defined as yaw zero relative to the rig root**, not computed from the agents. The User vertex already faces the triad centroid, which for the equilateral layout is the agents' midpoint; measured 0.32 degrees off, which is the agents' own head asymmetry under mocap rather than a layout error. That makes the recentring deterministic instead of depending on which mocap frame it happens to catch, and `Set Up XR Rig` now warns if the vertex ever drifts more than 3 degrees off, so the assumption cannot rot silently.

- 2026-08-27 — **The participant's viewpoint is a fixed 3D point: rotation tracks, translation does not** (user's call, extending the eye-height decision below to all three axes). `TrackedPoseDriver` is `RotationOnly`, so the headset never writes a position and nothing has to run afterwards to undo one — which also deleted the per-frame pin built an hour earlier.
  - **What it buys is a stimulus that is identical for everyone.** Height was only one of the axes: a participant who drifted 20 cm forward stood at 0.8 m from the agents instead of 1.0 m, changing the visual angle a gaze shift subtends — and how clearly a gaze shift reads is the dependent variable. It also makes the agents' *rendered* gaze deterministic, since they aim at this camera; under positional tracking their eye rotations differed per participant and differed from every desktop preview.
  - **The cost is no positional parallax**, and it is a real one: leaning does not move the view, and rotation is applied at the eyes rather than about the neck, so the world pivots slightly more than a body expects. This is ordinary 3DOF viewing and the task is 20-30 s of standing and watching, but it is recorded here as a **pilot question rather than a settled one**. If it needs fixing, a neck-pivot model restores most of the parallax while keeping the geometry identical across participants, because it depends only on head rotation and not on the body wearing the headset. Safety note: a participant who walks gets no visual feedback that they have, so the operator stays in the room.
  - `EyeHeightCalibration` became `ParticipantEyeHeight` — nothing is calibrated any more, and a class named for a step that no longer exists is exactly the drift this board is for. The constant and the 1.20-2.10 m plausibility bounds survive, now used only to decide whether a height read off the headset device is a standing participant or a headset on a desk.

- 2026-08-27 — **The participant's view is pinned at the agents' eye line every frame, and per-participant eye-height calibration is deleted** (user's call, choosing between pinning Y outright and auto-calibrating once). Two separate faults in what was there: the height was **1.60 m**, a generic adult eye height inherited from wherever the flat camera happened to sit, which left the participant **8.5 cm below** both agents; and it was only correct if an operator remembered to run `Calibrate()`, which has still never been run on real hardware.
  - **The height is now the SMPL-X model's own, measured rather than guessed.** `left/right_eye_smplhf` sit at 1.6846 m in the rest pose, and a 1,200-frame clip driven through the motion player puts them at mean 1.6815, range 1.663-1.713 — 3 mm from the rest-pose value, so a fixed height is level with the agents to within their own postural sway.
  - **Every frame beats once**, which is what makes height *irrelevant* rather than merely *corrected*: no step to forget, no sample taken while someone is mid-movement, and no window at the start of a session where the stimulus is wrong by however tall the participant happens to be. The accepted cost is vestibular: crouching no longer lowers the view. Acceptable for a stand-and-watch task of 20-30 s where vertical motion is a few centimetres of sway; a protocol with real vertical movement should freeze the offset after one sample instead.
  - **Flat and headset now share one height**, so a desktop preview frames the triad exactly as a worn take does. Safe to change because **no policy reads scene geometry**: the one field that did, `ConversationState.MutualGazeActive`, has gone unread since mutual-gaze breaking was dropped on 2026-07-30, so the 15 baked tracks are untouched and need no re-bake.
  - `EyeHeightCalibration`'s arithmetic and its 1.20-2.10 m plausibility bounds survive and are still the tested core — a rejected sample now **holds the previous offset** instead of leaving a stale calibration, because tracking dropping out must not yank the view to the floor.

- 2026-08-27 — **The participant's gaze goes into its own file on the decision grid, and mutual gaze is measured by head spheres.** §7 asked for the human's gaze "at the decision rate, alongside the 20-column agent log", and the tempting reading was to fill `mutual_gaze_with_human` in that log and be done. Rejected: the agent log is per **frame** and records what was *rendered*, the participant's gaze is per **tick** and records what was *decided against*, so one file would have to put one of the two on the wrong clock — and it would silently redefine a column the July analysis contract already fixed. `<stem>_user.csv` sits beside it with the same stem, and the sidecar says how the halves differ.
  - **Head spheres rather than the agent side's 15° cone**, because an angle subtends a different amount of head at every distance and the participant can step around the play area. That makes the two directions of mutual gaze incommensurate by construction, so `target_angle_deg` and the raw world-space ray are both logged and both thresholds are written into the sidecar — the threshold is an analysis choice on a finished log, not a decision baked into the take.
  - **`agents_looking_at_user` is logged as a bit set** even though it duplicates the agent log, so gaze-return latency (§7.4, the measure most specific to this setup) is computable from one file at one rate instead of a cross-rate join. It is read from the rendered eye bones, up to one frame stale at 90 Hz — ~11 ms against latencies of hundreds — because reading the commanded target instead would breach §5.1.
  - **A `StudySession` now refuses to start with no participant gaze logger wired.** Same argument as the other three integrity rules: a participant run with no objective gaze record looks entirely normal and is worth nothing.
  - Deliberately **not** built: the four derived measures. They are whole-take statistics over the captured files and belong in offline analysis, not in a component that runs during a trial.

- 2026-08-27 — **Questionnaire items are displayed in VR and answered aloud; the experimenter enters them on the desktop** (user's call). `user-study-design.md` §5 had specced a controller pointer, which is the reason §9.3 was estimated as "likely more work than the XR port itself". Dropping it removes XRI, the whole interaction layer, and a SteamVR controller path that has never been run under the Varjo loader — on hardware that has already produced one enumeration surprise. What is left in the headset is a world-space canvas with no input, and the entry surface is an IMGUI panel on the desktop, which the mirror shows and the eye textures do not.
  - **The accepted cost is demand effects**: twenty spoken answers per participant with the experimenter in the room. Mitigated in the protocol rather than in code — read the item verbatim, take the number, acknowledge with nothing beyond "thank you" — and by blinding the operator panel so the experimenter does not know which version is the interesting one while they are speaking. Written into `user-study-design.md` §6.1.
  - Design in `Assets/Docs/questionnaire-ui-design.md`; §6's instrument (items, scale, ranking, settled 2026-08-21) is unchanged and was not reopened.

- 2026-08-27 (latest) — **The XR backend is the Varjo Unity XR plugin, not OpenXR** (user's call, after the headset was connected). The port was built and verified against OpenXR on a portability argument, and that path *renders* correctly on the real headset — `Varjo OpenXR Runtime 4.14.0`, stereo, Floor origin, head pose driving the camera, **90 fps** with two SMPL-X agents plus correctives and LipSync, which closes the frame-rate risk the design flagged. What OpenXR would not deliver is gaze: `XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction` was **available and enabled on the instance**, yet no eye-tracking device ever appeared (`GetDevicesWithCharacteristics(EyeTracking)` = 0, nothing exposing `eyesData`, the `EyeGazeInteraction` feature reading disabled at runtime). Varjo's plugin also gives more than the extension does — per-eye rays, pupil size, focus distance against one combined ray — so §7's four measures will be built on `VarjoEyeTracking`.
  - `com.varjo.xr` (from Varjo's GitHub) is installed and is the **active Standalone loader**; `com.unity.xr.openxr` stays installed but inactive with its feature set intact, so the loader can be switched back cheaply. `XrParticipantRig` needs no change either way — it drives `XRGeneralSettings.Manager`, which is loader-agnostic.
  - **Nothing has been run through the Varjo loader yet.** Every measurement above is the OpenXR path; the loader switch came after them. First job next session: press Play with the Varjo loader and confirm stereo, tracking and a gaze source, then run `Calibrate()` on a worn headset — it has still never seen a real standing participant.
  - Worth checking before blaming code when gaze is missing: Varjo Base's eye-tracking permission, Varjo's own per-wearer ET calibration, and whether the headset is actually being worn (the proximity sensor can gate gaze). The headset was on the desk during today's probes.

- 2026-08-27 (latest) — **The decision grid now owns the clock, and all fifteen tracks were re-baked on the fix** (user's call). `ConversationDirector` no longer pulls a live clock delegate on every read: `GazeConditionRunner` calls `SyncTo(k · step)` once per decision tick, so time-to-boundary, time-since-boundary and turn phase are measured on the grid rather than at whatever sub-frame instant the frame clock happened to hold, and `ConversationState.Time` carries the tick's instant instead of Play's session clock (it was reporting `_sessionTime`, which was the wrong clock twice over). The director also stopped advancing in its own `Update`, which removes the ordering hazard the delegate existed for — it is driven by the one component that knows which instant is being decided at.
  - **Verified before re-baking anything**: two consecutive bakes of `study_c5` / Proposed / seed 4 are byte-identical apart from `bakedAtUtc` — **0 differing ticks of 2,836**, against 4 the day before — and the bake lands on the offline scan's prediction exactly (A 0.5028 / B 0.6671). 170/170 tests green.
  - The remaining scan-vs-bake gap is arithmetic, not disagreement: the scan simulates `ceil((duration + tail)/step)` ticks while a bake stops when the conversation finishes, so when `duration × 60` is not an integer the scan counts one extra trailing tick (`study_c1`: 448/1315 baked against 449/1316 scanned). Inside their shared ticks they agree.
  - The aggregate barely moved — `study_c1` Proposed went 0.3412 → 0.3407 aversion — so this buys reproducibility, not different behaviour. That is the point: "here is the seed that produced this stimulus" is now a claim that regenerates the file.
  - **All fifteen tracks re-baked and validated**: right segment, right condition, 60 Hz, seed matching the filename, sample count exactly duration × 60, timestamps monotone. Aversion over the ten agent-clips is Proposed **26.8-66.7%**, baseline A **34.5-58.3%**, baseline B zero — the same spread as before, so §3's reported numbers and the twelve-seed scan table stand unchanged (means, sds, ranges and all ten ranks recomputed identical).
  - **Scan and bake now agree tick for tick on every clip, condition and agent.** The only differences left are the one extra trailing tick the scan simulates where `duration × 60` is not an integer (4 of 20 agent-tracks), and inside the shared ticks the counts are equal. Before the fix the same comparison was off by up to a tenth of a point.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **The study runs on a Varjo through OpenXR, tethered, and XR never starts by itself** (user's call on the hardware; the rest follows from it). OpenXR rather than the Varjo XR plugin because Varjo's runtime exposes the eye-gaze extension through the standard, so the study depends on `XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction` rather than one vendor's plugin version and survives a change of headset. Tethered rather than standalone because every `segment.json` points motion at `F:\Data\...` on the lab machine and because SMPL-X's 486 correctives plus LipSync on two agents is desktop-CPU work.
  - **Auto-initialisation is off, deliberately.** Baking tracks, browsing clips and recording videos all press Play on a machine that may have no headset; "Initialize XR on Startup" would break every one of them. `XrParticipantRig.StartXrOnPlay` is the only switch, false in the committed scene, and flat mode parks the camera at 1.60 m — the exact pose every existing recording used, so the port changes no desktop take.
  - **Eye height is normalised, not merely tolerated.** The agents aim at the participant's real head either way (the human's `LookAtAnchor` is the tracked camera, so nothing in the gaze pipeline needed changing), but the *stimulus* geometry would differ per participant: fixed-height mocap agents mean a 1.50 m participant looks up and a 1.90 m one looks down, and how clearly a gaze shift reads is what the study measures. `Calibrate()` moves the play area so every participant's eyes sit at 1.60 m, rejects samples outside 1.20-2.10 m rather than clamping them (the headset on the desk), and re-measures rather than stacking on a second call. The raw height is kept for the participant record.
  - Verified only under the OpenXR **mock runtime** — subsystems up, floor origin, stereo, HMD device, and a simulated 1.85 m participant calibrated to exactly 1.600 m. A Varjo has not been attached.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **Proposed bakes are not bit-reproducible at 60 Hz, and the board's earlier "byte-identical" claim is withdrawn.** Found while regression-testing the XR port: re-baking `study_c5` / Proposed / seed 4 moved 2 ticks of 1,418, so the port was suspected. It is not the port — **five bakes all differ from each other**, including a back-to-back pair run under matched editor settings (4 differing ticks of 2,836, i.e. two agents × 1,418), at the same place each time: t ≈ 3.3-3.5 s, inside a prototype window, a single tick flipping between a person and an aversion. Seeds, sample counts and every other tick are identical, and the aversion fraction moves by at most **0.14 points**, so the reported §3 numbers stand.
  - Cause: `ProposedGazePolicy` reads its position in the prototype from `state.PredictedTimeToTurnEnd`, which the director derives from the **frame's** conversation clock. `DecisionClock` fixes which frame tick *k* runs on but not the sub-frame remainder of that frame's reading, so a one-frame prototype segment is sampled or missed depending on frame timing. At 30 Hz a tick spanned two prototype frames and filtered this out — which is why the 2026-08-25 byte-identical result was true when it was measured, and stopped being true when the tick moved to 60 Hz the next day.
  - Consequence for the study: **none for the stimulus** — the tracks are committed files and every participant sees the same one; the validated `study_c5` track was restored after the test. What is not true is "a re-bake regenerates a track bit-for-bit". The fix, if wanted, is to hand policies the tick's nominal time (*k · step*) instead of the frame's clock — exactly what the offline seed scan already does. It would make scan and bake agree exactly rather than to a tenth of a point, and it re-opens all fifteen tracks for a re-bake. Not done: it is the user's call whether the claim is worth another bake round.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **The seed scan now sweeps baseline A as well as Proposed, and the study's spread is measured for both.** The scan had covered the proposed condition only, which looked for an unlucky draw in one half of the comparison while baseline A samples dwells and jump targets of its own — and scene 2 had already produced a baseline A take that averted 100% of a hold. `SeedScan.Run` takes the condition; the Clip Browser sweeps both in one press; baseline B is refused rather than scanned, because it carries no random stream and reads voice activity rather than the schedule, and the scan runs in silence.
  - **Validated against ground truth exactly as the Proposed scan was**: scanning baseline A at each clip's baked seed reproduces the baked track on **all five clips and both agents to within 0.05 percentage points** of aversion. So a baseline A take is determined by its seed the way a Proposed one is — the open item in `user-study-design.md` §10 saying A "was not tested the same way" is closed.
  - **The spread, over seeds 1-12 × five clips × two agents (120 agent-takes per condition):** Proposed mean 41.5%, sd 11.2 points, range 18.0-67.9%; baseline A mean 44.7%, sd **8.7** points, range 21.8-61.8%. Baseline A is stochastic but *less* variable, which is what the mechanisms predict — it samples many short dwells while holding replay draws whole stretches with a long-tailed length distribution.
  - **The arbitrary seeds behaved like arbitrary seeds**, which is the empirical form of the 2026-08-26 decision below. Ranking each baked draw within its own clip × agent distribution of twelve gives mean rank 7.0 (Proposed) and 6.5 (baseline A) against the 6.5 expected of uniform draws, and the ten ranks cover 1 to 12 in both conditions.
  - **Nothing in the baked set is pathological, and the flagged case is confirmed as a tail.** `study_c5`'s agent B under Proposed (66.6%) is rank 12 of 12. Baseline A's most extreme draws are `study_c2` and `study_c5`, where one agent sits at the bottom of its twelve and the other near the top — an unbalanced *pair* rather than one checked-out agent. Over all 240 scanned agent-takes the maximum is 67.9%; scene 2's 100% does not recur.
  - Not re-baked and no seed re-picked: per the decision below the seeds stay unselected. The scan is for reporting the spread, not for choosing.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **The study's seeds are unselected and recorded, not chosen from the middle of a scan** (user's call, after asking what would actually be wrong with the arbitrary ones). They are right that this is the stronger position: fairness requires only that the choice carry no information about the resulting take, and it demonstrably did not — the broken scan's numbers correlate with the real ones at **r = +0.20**. So the original seeds (8/4/7/7/4) were a legitimate arbitrary draw, and "the base seed was fixed arbitrarily and recorded" is a sentence that needs no defending, unlike a selection rule.
  - The median-seed set baked earlier (10/9/3/6/11) was deleted and the arbitrary seeds re-baked. Both were reproducible, so this cost only time.
  - **It also avoids a contradiction with the 2026-08-21 decision**, which wanted the condition *sampled* rather than exemplified. With five conversations there are five natural draws; median-picking all five would have removed exactly that variability and shown the method without its tail.
  - The accepted cost: `study_c5`'s agent B averts **66.6%** — looking away for two thirds of a 24 s clip. Flagged, not fixed. `Assets/Docs/user-study-design.md` §3 now says to report the twelve-seed scan spread alongside the results, so a reader sees the condition's variability rather than inferring consistency from five draws.
  - Worth keeping straight: **the seed scan does not change any probability.** Once baked a take is deterministic; the scan only decides which point of the condition's distribution gets exhibited. It is a representativeness choice, not a statistical correction — and nobody has yet shown that aversion fraction is what drives the naturalness ranking, so it is a proxy either way.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **Baseline B is not bit-reproducible across bakes; the other two conditions are.** Re-baking all five clips at identical seeds reproduced four exactly and moved `study_c4` by 19 ticks (0.32 s). Its input is the audio playback position, scheduled against the DSP clock, so *when the first voice onset is confirmed* can land either side of the decision grid — it changes only how long the agents watch the participant before anyone has spoken. Harmless for a study session, since participants replay the file, but "a bake is regenerable" holds bit-for-bit only for the schedule-driven conditions.

- 2026-08-26 (later) — **The decision tick is 60 Hz, not 30** (user's question, then their call). Nothing had ever justified 30: `baseline-spec.md` §0.2 said "20-50 Hz is plenty" and argued only for *decoupling* decisions from the frame rate. Both data sources are 60 fps, so 60 Hz is one tick per recorded frame — the prototypes are 1 s windows of 60 frames and now map 1:1, and the holding corpus's fixation durations are exact multiples of 1/60 s. Measured over the bank's 7,150 durations: **mean rounding error 8.17 ms at 30 Hz against 0.02 ms at 60**. `HoldingReplayGazePolicy` already carried a workaround comment for that quantisation. Cost is 2× ticks (~1,400 samples per agent per clip) and it re-opens every seed, which is why it was settled before baking rather than after.
  - Also measured: 13% of prototype segments are shorter than one 30 Hz tick. Most of that is label flicker — 8 of the 10 interior sub-tick segments have the same target either side, e.g. `None → CurrentSpeaker(1 frame) → None`, which 30 Hz usefully filtered out — but 2 are real brief transitions that it dropped or shifted.

- 2026-08-26 (later) — **Baseline B could never be baked or replayed, and nobody had noticed.** Found by the user watching a bake: agent B stared at the participant for the whole take. One cause, two symptoms. `TryPrepareCondition` returned early for `SpeakerFollowing` — it needs no director — **before** the block that allocates the bake recorders and loads a replay track. So baking baseline B threw `NullReferenceException` on every tick and wrote no file, and because the throw happened at *agent A's* recorder line it aborted the tick before agent B was reached, leaving agent B on its Awake-initialised target (the human) forever. Replay was equally broken: `_track` was never loaded for it. All three study conditions could not have run from tracks.
  - The early return now guards only the director requirement. Baseline B bakes correctly: A→B 97%, B→A 97%, user 2% — matching the documented expectation.
  - **The stare was a symptom of a crash, not of the audio levels**, which is the failure it resembles (`CLAUDE.md` records the −42 dBFS case where baseline B detects no speech and both agents watch the user). Worth remembering: the two look identical on screen.

- 2026-08-26 (latest) — **The seed scan was sweeping every seed through one director that cannot rewind.** `ConversationDirector.SyncToClock` only ever walks `_index` *forward* — correct for a live conversation, which never goes back — but `SeedScan.Run` reused a single director across all twelve seeds and reset only the clock. So the **first seed scanned was right and every later one ran the entire simulation against a schedule frozen on the final turn.** That is the whole discrepancy: yesterday's `cand_v008` check passed because it scanned a *single* seed, one forward sweep; the twelve-seed scans used to pick the study clips were reading frozen roles for eleven of twelve seeds.
  - Found by replaying the scan tick-by-tick against a baked track: agent A matched the bake to 0.1 point and agent B diverged at tick 197 — the second pass over the same director.
  - Fixed by re-publishing the schedule per seed (`SetSchedule` calls `Enter(0)`). **Verified against ground truth: the scan now reproduces all five baked clips on both agents to a tenth of a point.**
  - **All five seeds had to be re-picked and the clips re-baked.** Every seed chosen from the broken scan (8/4/7/7/4) was a non-first seed, so all five were chosen from frozen-role numbers. The corrected picks are 10/9/3/6/11, and they are visibly better balanced — Proposed aversion 29-47% across the ten agent-clips against 26.8-66.7% before.
  - Worth remembering as a class: **a monotone helper reused across simulation runs is a stateful object pretending to be a pure function.** The first run is always right, which is exactly what makes it hard to see.

- 2026-08-26 (later) — ~~**The seed scan is not a predictor and the docs said it was.**~~ **Cause found and fixed the same day — see the entry above.** Recorded because the measurement stands: Over the five study clips it missed the baked aversion fraction by up to **25 percentage points** (`study_c1` agent B: predicted 52%, baked 26.8%; `study_c5` agent A: predicted 31%, baked 50.3%), having matched `cand_v008` exactly on 2026-08-25. `SeedScan.BuildState` assembles its own `ConversationState` rather than the runner's — partners from `Speakers` with a `User` fallback instead of the triad, `MutualGazeActive` hard-coded false — and one different early draw cascades, because holding stretches average ~4 s. Cause not isolated. §10 now says a bake is the ground truth and a scan only ranks seeds; the claim that they "agree exactly" is withdrawn.
  - Consequence for the baked set: the five seeds were chosen on those numbers, so they are not reliably mid-spread. `study_c5` agent B averts 66.7%, near the top of the distribution.

- 2026-08-26 (later) — **A bake now gives up rather than hanging.** `GazeTrackBaker` stopped play on `HasFinished`, which a conversation that never started never reaches, so a segment Unity had not imported left it in Play Mode indefinitely — ten minutes of silence before anyone looked. It now abandons the queue with an error after 30 s without the conversation's clock starting. The trigger was exporting clips from the shell without refreshing the AssetDatabase; the wavs existed on disk but `AssetDatabase.LoadAssetAtPath` returned null.

- 2026-08-26 — **The study's five clips are `036`, `040`, `081`, `119`, `120`** (user's pick from their own shortlist of eight). Twelve EoT events, all three classes, seven distinct speakers. Written up in `Assets/Docs/scene1-clip-candidates.md`, which now leads with the decision rather than the shortlist, and named in `user-study-design.md` §3.

Same-speaker control 0.837-0.973 against a cross-clip median of 0.130: two populations, wide gap. Result: **seven speakers across the eight surviving clips, one woman in six of them**, `008`/`050`/`119` are the same two women and `026`/`036` the same two men. So the shortlist held only **five distinct casts**, and one clip from each was the whole degree of freedom.

Its exchange is a monologue with backchannels (balance 0.57) and its content is a tsunami story; flagged for the pilot.

The symptom was the bug. With the cap gone, person fixations render at 21-33° and the contrast against a recentred aversion is plainly visible, which is what the earlier concern was really about.

A live run at that seed commands 0.0/0.0 aversion on both agents again. 161/161 tests green with the three `…RecentresTheEyesInTheHead` assertions restored.
