- 2026-08-25 (latest) — **The gaze animation layer was frame-rate dependent, and every live session rendered a fraction of the gaze the policy asked for.** Reported by the user watching `case1_seg02` through the Clip Browser: "nearly no eye movement for both agents, especially agent A" — while the 2026-08-14 recording of the same clip looks right. It is not the policy. Same clip, same seed, identical decisions, only the frame rate differing: agent A's aversion renders **12.7°/7.5° at 30 fps and 1.4°/1.1° at 280 fps** against a commanded 14.4°/8.4°; the eyes sit within 3° of centre 71% of the take instead of 41%.
  - **Cause.** `RecordedConversation.Update` seeks the motion every frame, `SmplxAnimUtils.SetPose` writes all 55 joints, and the TalkingWithHands clips carry **no eye animation at all** — `left_eye`/`right_eye` axis-angles are exactly 0.000 on every frame (so is `jaw`), measured straight off the corpus `.npz`. So the mocap resets both eye bones to identity every frame, and `GazeController` integrated from that reset pose: the rendered angle could never exceed one frame's rotation, `EyeDegreesPerSecond / fps`. **20° at the recorder's locked 30 fps** — which is why every recorded take looks right and hid this for months — but **2.1° live at 280 fps** and **6.7° in 90 Hz VR, which is what the study runs on**. The head bone already had a guard for exactly this (`_writtenHeadLocal`/`_baseHeadLocal`); the eyes had none.
  - **Fix.** `GazeController` resumes each eye from its own last written local rotation instead of from whatever the mocap left — the layer owns the eye bones, which is what `CLAUDE.md` already claims. The world target is still recomputed per frame, so VOR is unchanged. Verified: at ~280 fps aversion now renders 13.9°/8.6° against 14.3°/8.8° commanded (97%), and time within 3° of centre falls from 71% to 4%. 161/161 tests green.
  - **The old takes were clipped, not merely quiet.** The 20°/frame cap silently truncated any target more than 20° from the head's forward, so agent B looking at **the human** rendered 20.0° and now reaches **33.3°**, up against the ±35° eye clamp. Every existing comparison recording under-shows gaze at the user; the set needs re-recording before it is shown to anyone.
  - **Open question this exposes:** with `HeadContribution = 0` the head never turns and the user sits ~60° off each agent's facing direction, so gaze at the user is **pegged at the yaw clamp**. Whether that reads as "being looked at" in VR is exactly what the study's "seemed aware I was there" item measures — worth settling in the pilot rather than by argument.
  - **Not covered by a unit test.** `GazeController` lives in `Assembly-CSharp`, which no asmdef test assembly can reference, so the only tested code is the policy layer. This was caught by measuring two live runs against each other, and that is currently the only way to catch it. Moving the animation layer into its own asmdef would fix that.

- 2026-08-25 (latest) — **The decision grid is anchored on the conversation's clock, which closes the reproducibility blocker.** `DecisionClock` (in the policy assembly, so it is unit-tested) replaces the runner's free-running accumulator: it reports no tick while the clock reads negative, and tick *k* is the first frame at or after *k · step* of conversation. The suspected mechanism was the mechanism — the pre-roll's length varies with load time, and every pre-roll tick spent a draw. **Verified by baking twice, not only in tests:** two bakes of `cand_v008` / Proposed / seed 8 are byte-identical apart from `bakedAtUtc` (706 samples per agent; 41/41 and 56/56 episodes), on the seeds that diverged before. 161/161 tests green.
  - **Ticks are stamped with grid time, not the clock reading they fired on.** The frame a conversation starts on is regularly longer than a step — Unity clamps it to `maximumDeltaTime` — so the opening burst of ~11 decisions all fell due at one reading. The first bake recorded eleven samples at t = 0.3333 and a track that was not strictly monotone; stamped with grid time the track opens at 0.000 and steps cleanly, and two bakes then agree on timestamps as well as decisions.
  - **The offline seed scan and the live runner now agree exactly**, which they could not before — `SeedScan` has always ticked at `t = k · step` from conversation zero, so anchoring the live grid the same way made them the same grid. Scanned seed 8 on `cand_v008` predicts aversion 0.596 / 0.516; the bake of that configuration measures 421/706 = 0.596 and 364/706 = 0.516. Picking a clip's seed from a scan is sound now, rather than an approximation to check by recording.
  - **Residual, and the standing reason a study replays a baked track:** a tick reads the live scene at the frame it fires on, so voice activity and a turn boundary can still land one frame either side of the grid. Baking removes that; nothing in a live take can, because baseline B's voice detection reads the audio at playback position by design.
  - Pre-roll now renders as the initial target applied once, rather than as decisions nobody sees. `RecordedConversation.Elapsed` was already the right clock to anchor on — it is `Time.time` since the segment started, so it accumulates exactly as the old accumulator did, only from the right origin.

- 2026-08-25 (latest) — **Two bake bugs found while verifying the above, both of which could silently cost a take.** Neither was caused by the pre-roll change; both were found because the verification needed two clean bakes in a row.
  - **`GazeTrackBaker` never left Play Mode for the last queued condition.** Its "is a bake running" test was "the queue is not empty", but the queue is emptied when the *final* condition starts — so the last session (which is the only session, for Bake Current Condition) ran forever, the track was written only if someone stopped play by hand, and `Finish` never ran, leaving the scene in **Bake** where the next Play would overwrite what it had just made. Now a separate `Active` session key. This is the same class as the `[Serializable]` null-check bug: a sentinel that cannot distinguish "finished" from "nothing to do".
  - **A bake could throw its own track away on the way out.** The track is written in `OnDestroy`, which reads the participants' names and the conversation's segment — and Unity gives no destruction order, so a destroyed `GazeParticipant` threw `MissingReferenceException` out of the writer (observed: one bake produced no file at all) while a destroyed conversation would have read as null and written a track naming no segment, to the fallback path rather than beside its clip. The header is now captured in `Start` and the track is also committed when the conversation finishes, with `OnDestroy` left as the early-stop fallback.

- 2026-08-25 (later) — **The study replays a baked gaze track rather than re-deriving a take** (user's call, after asking whether fixed seeds would do). They would not: the two runs that diverged already had **identical** seeds, so the seed was never what was broken — *when* the draws get consumed was. Baking also buys something seeding structurally cannot: the stimulus stops depending on the code. Gaze behaviour changed twice on 2026-08-24/25; had that happened mid-collection, early and late participants would have seen different stimuli with nothing to signal it. `GazeTrack` (JSON beside its segment), `BakedGazePolicy`, and `GazeConditionRunner.Tracks` = Off / Bake / Replay.
  - **Samples are stamped with conversation time, not tick index.** That is the fix, not a detail: indexing by tick reproduces the original bug, because the runner ticks from Play start while the conversation clock starts only once the segment loads. Time-indexing is immune to load time, frame rate and tick alignment together. Two guards fall out — the first decision is held while the clock reads negative (a slow load cannot eat the opening), and the cursor never rewinds on a stall (a backwards gaze jump would also break the log's monotonicity).
  - Baking runs the **real** play path, not an offline simulation: it is what a study session replays, and baseline B's voice detection reads the audio at playback position, which an offline harness would have to reimplement and could get subtly wrong.
  - **Valid only because no policy input depends on the human** — voice from the agents' own clips, schedule from the segment, mutual gaze from the agents' rendered eye bones. Written into `GazeTrack`'s summary as the condition to revisit if an agent is ever made to react to the participant's gaze.
  - `GazeTrackBaker` queues all three conditions through consecutive play sessions (`SessionState`, the `DemoRecorder` pattern) and restores the scene's mode afterwards, so a bake cannot leave the scene in Bake where the next Play would overwrite what it just made. The Clip Browser shows which conditions have a track for the current seed.
  - ~~**The pre-roll fix is still open**~~ — done the same day, see the 2026-08-25 (latest) decision below. A bake is regenerable now, which is what "here is the seed that produced this stimulus" needs to be a reproducible claim in the paper.

- 2026-08-25 (later) — **`GazeConditionRunner.StudySession` refuses to start a run that must not be shown to a participant.** One switch enforcing every integrity rule at once, because each failure produces a normal-looking session that is quietly worthless: gaze decided live (a different stimulus from every other participant), logging off (no record), or the developer overlay on (it names the very boundaries the questionnaire asks about). Verified by probing all combinations — and it caught the overlay switched on in the working scene on its first real check.
  - **A bug it exposed in itself:** the "is a track loaded" test was `_track == null`, which never fired. `GazeTrack` is `[Serializable]`, so Unity hands such a field a *default-constructed* instance instead of leaving it null — the guard's most important check was silently passing with no track. Fixed with `[NonSerialized]` plus an `agents.Length == 0` test, and re-verified. Worth remembering as a class of bug: a null check on a `[Serializable]` field is not a null check.

- 2026-08-25 — ~~**Every condition now renders aversion the same way: a sampled direction from baseline A's fitted table.**~~ **Reverted the same day — see the latest entry. Kept here because the reasoning is still on the record and the reversal turns on one measurement, not on a change of mind.** The proposed condition used to recentre the eyes for both the prototypes' `None` and the holding substrate's aversion fixations. Caught by the user watching three candidates and reporting "the eyes are just centered": the logs showed the policy choosing aversion for 42-65% of a take and every one of those frames rendering at exactly (0, 0). With `HeadContribution = 0` the head is pure mocap, so a recentred agent is indistinguishable from one with no gaze control at all — and the study's primary DV is a ranking of *"how natural the characters' eye movements were"*, which participants would have answered on the rendering rather than on the policy. **This reverses the 2026-08-02 call** (made twice), and the ground had moved under it: that decision governed the prototypes' `None` inside a 1 s window against a substrate that still averted directionally, whereas since 2026-08-14 the holding substrate recentred too, so the condition had no directional aversion anywhere. Restores `baseline-spec.md` §0.1 — one animation layer, all conditions — by construction rather than by discipline.
  - `HoldingReplayGazePolicy` and `ProposedGazePolicy` each take `ShintaniGazeParameters` and own an `AversionSampler`; the runner loads the fitted parameters for `Proposed` as well as `RoleConditioned` now. The aversion stream is **per-agent**, unlike the prototype draw both agents share: which prototype fires at a boundary must be coordinated, which way an agent looks away must not.
  - Consecutive aversion fixations continue one aversion rather than re-drawing a direction each time. The sampler re-targets on its own measured 0.7 s period; the split between two adjacent aversion fixations is an artifact of how the corpus event table tiles the timeline, not a gaze event.
  - 144/144 tests green. Seven failed first — all asserting the old behaviour. The three `…RecentresTheEyesInTheHead` tests were rewritten as `…LooksAwayInASampledDirection`; four others where the zero offset was incidental (fixation ordering, role-change handover, substrate delegation) now compare target type and person instead of the whole `GazeTarget`.

- 2026-08-25 — **The proposed condition is stochastic, was described as deterministic, and its per-take variance is large.** The board's "one recording *is* the condition rather than one draw from it" was true under the baseline-B substrate (no random stream) and stopped being true on 2026-08-14 when holding replay landed; nobody re-checked. Replaying the draw rule 20,000 times over a real role plan gives an aversion fraction with **mean 39%, sd 13 percentage points** over a 25 s take — a 5-95% range of roughly 20% to 62%. The cause is structural: bank stretches have a median of ~2.4 s but a mean of ~4 s and maxima of 90-170 s, so one long aversion stretch can swallow a quarter of a clip. **Consequences: the study seeds Proposed per participant × conversation exactly like baseline A** (`Assets/Docs/user-study-design.md` §2), and clips must be chosen with the seed scan rather than by watching whichever seed the scene was left on.
  - The user's "still centered most of the time" take was measured at the ~95th percentile for aversion — a genuinely unlucky draw, not a bug.

- 2026-08-25 — **BLOCKER found: the proposed condition does not reproduce run to run.** Two runs of `cand_v014` with identical segment, condition and per-agent seeds gave AgentB an identical decision sequence (27/27 episodes) while AgentA diverged at episode 6. So the recorded seed does not fully determine a take: it cannot be re-recorded identically, and the sidecar's seed is not sufficient provenance. Suspected mechanism (unconfirmed): the runner ticks policies from Play start while the conversation clock only starts once the segment has loaded, so a variable-length pre-roll consumes draws. Recorded in the study design doc §10 as a prerequisite to fix before any data collection.

- 2026-08-21 — **The study is scene 1 only, in live VR with eye tracking, ranking-first** (user's calls across the design discussion). Five conversations × three methods, every participant seeing all fifteen, blocked by conversation so the three versions can be ranked against each other. **Scene 2 is discarded from the study for now** — its "did you feel invited to speak" measure rests on the participant feeling addressed by a corpus question that was spoken to the other agent, and the user's own report was that it did not land. The platform question parked since 2026-07-13 is answered: VR, live scene, not video on a screen.
  - Ranking is the primary DV rather than absolute Likert: participants may not know how to score gaze on a scale, and a ranking is immune to scale-use bias and much more sensitive to a gaze-only difference. The cost — participants knowingly compare three versions of one conversation and may hunt for differences — is standard for within-subjects gaze work and is detected by the manipulation and demand checks rather than designed away.
  - **Items must name eye movements, never "behaviour"**: motion is identical across methods, so any item admitting motion has participants partly rating a constant. This cut two drafted items (overall believability; predicting the next speaker) — the second also because the paper's position is that gaze alone cannot predict turns, and the participant never takes a turn, so there is nothing behavioural to validate it against.
  - **The framing says "you are the third person in this conversation" and stops there** — telling participants they might be looked at primes the one item with the sharpest prediction (baseline B never looks at the user; Proposed gives them 4-50% of out-of-window gaze) and reads as strange. An unprompted effect is the stronger result.

- 2026-08-21 — **Baseline A is seeded per participant × conversation, not fixed across the study.** It is the only stochastic condition, so a fixed seed lets one draw stand in for the whole condition — and an unlucky draw has already been observed (in `case2_seg02` A happened to avert 100% of the hold, which would have been reported as the baseline's behaviour). Per-participant seeding samples the condition properly across the 30 participants while staying exactly reproducible, and the variance is absorbed by the participant random effect. Every seed goes in the take's sidecar.

- 2026-08-21 — **Study clips may be any voice mix, and mixed-gender pairs are preferred.** Texture follows the measured voices as before, but there is exactly **one stock albedo per sex**, so a same-sex pair forces one agent onto a SMPLitex texture and its known nostril misregistration — while a **mixed pair puts both agents on stock textures and is the only configuration free of the artifact entirely**. It is constant across the three methods of a conversation either way, so it can never be a confound; it only adds noise. This makes `--voice mixed` the preferred filter for clip selection rather than merely an allowed one.

- 2026-08-16 (later) — **Agent A wears the stock Meshcapade female albedo, not a SMPLitex one** (user's call, after spotting that the nostril texture sits below the nostrils on agent B too and inferring a UV problem). Swapping A to the stock atlas was both the fix and the experiment: the stock texture registers correctly on the same mesh, which rules the FBX's UVs out and puts the misregistration in SMPLitex's output. The cost is that A now wears the sample body rather than clothes, and that A and B no longer come from the same generator — accepted, because a visibly wrong face beats a matched pair at the distance the questionnaire asks people to judge gaze from.

- 2026-08-16 — **Agent A wears `SMPLitex-texture-00017`** (user's call, reviewing `case2_seg02`: the old texture "doesn't fit the body"). The replaced sample, `f00016`, was also the one carrying the yellow-green fingers and toes that no colour statistic could remove — the 2026-08-10 note already named swapping the sample as the only clean fix, so one swap settles both. The old PNG is deleted rather than kept beside the new one: it is unreferenced, git holds it, and an unused near-duplicate albedo in `Assets/SMPLX/Textures/` is exactly the thing that gets wired back in by accident. **Superseded the same day** by the decision above; `f00017` is left in the tree pending the user's call on whether to keep it.

- 2026-08-14 (later) — **Scene 2 windows must not contain internal turn-taking** (user's call): with no floor change in the lead-in, the user taking the turn violates no established dyadic rhythm — safe by construction; with one, whether joining feels abrupt depends on the conversation's semantics, which no timing feature can judge. So the default search admits monologue-with-backchannels windows only, `--allow-internal-events` admits interruptions/overlaps but never internal turn-takings, and any such candidate is judged by reading its `--inspect` transcript. Question-final closers outrank everything: the corpus transcripts are punctuated (1,743 `?` tokens), so "ends with a question" is a direct test, and an open question aimed at the camera is the clearest "your turn" pretext.

- 2026-08-14 (later) — **Scene 2 ships as a segment-authoring mode, not a new policy.** The user (speaker code 0, schema `/2`) is the final turn's taker; the existing prototype machinery fires the yield because the final turn carries a real event index; the one policy change is `TrackFor` playing the listener track for a participant in neither boundary role — data-safe (no prototype's listener track names the listener) and unreachable in scene-1 schedules. The hold after the voices stop is segment data (`tailSeconds`), read by the recorder.

- 2026-08-14 — **Scene 2 needs no turn-taking detection: the user never actually takes the turn** (user's call). After agent A's gaze implication the scene holds for a few seconds and ends; the dependent measure is the questionnaire ("did you feel you should take the turn?", gaze naturalness 1-5), not behaviour. This removes microphone/VAD-on-the-user and input handling from Scene 2's scope entirely. The step after Scene 2 is designing the user study method and questions.

- 2026-08-13 — **The Proposed condition's non-turn behaviour will be holding-period replay from our own corpus** (user's call, choosing between "tame baseline A" and "derive a non-turn model from our data"). Non-parametric replay was preferred over fitting a new parametric model: the event table tiles the timeline losslessly, so actual role-conditioned fixation sequences can be replayed verbatim — side-participant gaze and aversion time come out right by construction, with no dwell-law debate (chi-square and even lognormal fit these durations poorly). The reframe matters as much as the mechanism: the proposed method becomes *holding replay + EoT prototypes* as one full data-driven model, matching the project's ethos (corpus audio, corpus motion, corpus prototypes — now corpus sequences between them). **This will supersede the 2026-08-09 "substrate is baseline B" decision once implemented**; the isolated pattern-only contrast that decision bought is recovered by a prototype-off ablation, not by the substrate choice. Baselines A and B themselves stay untouched — a tuned baseline is not a baseline. Upstream data paths are now recorded in CLAUDE.md (Gaze control section).

- 2026-08-10 — **Case 1 replays a real TalkingWithHands conversation instead of a scripted TTS exchange** (user's call). The agents speak the corpus's own audio, move on its own mocap, and the gaze patterns fire on its annotated end-of-turn events. Kokoro TTS (`Assets/TTS/`, `KokoroTts`, `TtsSpeaker`) and `TriadConversation` are **deleted**, not left dormant — they were the only conversation source and dead code around a signed-off pipeline is worse than a git history lookup. What this buys the demo: real overlaps, backchannels and interruptions, boundaries that a human annotation pipeline found rather than ones we asserted, and a 24 s take with two hand-overs instead of a 12 s take with one.

- 2026-08-10 — **Every end-of-turn event fires a prototype drawn from its own class's pool** (user's call). All fifteen prototypes the paper prints are transcribed, so an interruption gets an interruption prototype and a turn-taking boundary gets a turn-taking one. Two consequences worth reporting: the proposed condition is no longer "one prototype, repeated", so a take exercises several of the paper's findings at once; and it is still fully deterministic, because the draw is a hash of the run's seed and the event index rather than a running random stream. **The pattern seed is the run's, not the agent's** — a per-agent seed would have each agent playing a different prototype's track at the other, which is the one way this could be quietly wrong.

- 2026-08-10 — **Segments are chosen by a documented, re-runnable filter rather than by eye.** `Tools/find_demo_segments.py` encodes what a usable demo segment is and ranks what survives. Two of its rules are worth keeping in mind when reading a take: utterances are rebuilt with the same 0.3 s pause split the event builder used, so segment boundaries agree with the events by construction; and backchannels are **not** dropped for boundary purposes even though the event builder drops them, because a boundary that cuts through "mm-hmm" still sounds like a cut.

- 2026-08-10 — **Exported segment audio is peak-normalised to 0.70, with one gain shared by both speakers.** The corpus records around −42 dBFS, far below anything the voice-activity detector's absolute-RMS threshold can see, so the raw levels made baseline B a constant stare at the human user. Normalising in the exporter rather than lowering the threshold fixes the demo's audibility at the same time and keeps the threshold calibrated in ordinary units. The gain is shared because the level difference between the two speakers is recorded, not incidental; it and the pre-gain peak are written into `segment.json` as provenance.

- 2026-08-10 (later) — **An agent speaking over the floor-holder addresses *them*, not the human.** This **supersedes** the fallback-to-human resolution adopted earlier the same day, which was correct that an agent is not its own addressee and wrong about where to send it instead. Talking while someone else holds the floor is what a backchannel is, so the case is common rather than exceptional, and the human fallback made an agent stare at the user for 66% of a take. §3's human fallback now applies only when neither `CurrentAddressee` nor `CurrentSpeaker` names anyone else. **Report baseline B as: look at the addressee, or at the floor-holder when the agent is talking over them.**
  - Worth remembering how it surfaced: the previous segment happened to have an agent that rarely backchannels, so the same bug cost 5% there and looked like rounding. Changing the material, not re-reading the code, is what exposed it.

- 2026-08-10 — **Speaker voice type is measured from the audio, because the corpus does not record it.** Median F0 per speaker over their own voiced frames, filterable as `--voice male|female|mixed`, stored in `segment.json`. Validated against a segment whose voices were known by ear. This is what makes "pick a two-male conversation" a query rather than a listening exercise, and it is what the agents' textures should be matched to.

- 2026-08-10 — **Baseline B's §3 rules now apply symmetrically to the agent itself.** Real conversation audio makes voice activity and the turn schedule disagree — backchannels, overlaps, early starts — and two gaps followed from that: `current_addressee` names whoever the *floor-holder* addresses, so it can name this agent (an agent is not its own addressee, and §3's fallback covers it); and backchannel suppression was applied only when switching *to* a partner, so the agent's own "yeah" still re-aimed it. Both are read out of §3 rather than invented, and neither could occur in the TTS demo where audio and schedule were the same thing. **Report baseline B as implementing §3's hysteresis uniformly across self and partners.**

- 2026-08-10 — **The recorded conversation runs on the frame clock, and that is a deliberate choice against the audio clock.** An audio-clock (`AudioSettings.dspTime`) version was implemented first, on the reasoning that a stalled player loop slides a frame-counted clock behind the voices — 3.5 s of divergence was measured in an editor session. It produced a take **0.7 s shorter than the segment with the last utterance clipped**, because Unity Recorder writes one output frame per rendered frame: the video's timeline *is* the frame count. Reverted. What was kept from the attempt: both voices are scheduled on a single DSP instant, and the conversation owns the one clock that motion, the turn schedule and every policy read.
  - The recorder also had to be made to **hold the segment until its encoder is up** (it clears its pending flag after `StartRecording`, and the conversation waits on that flag). Before this, the first **2.08 s** of the conversation was missing from every video — measured, not guessed, by cross-correlating the recorded audio against the source.

- 2026-08-09 — **The proposed method's substrate is Baseline B, not Baseline A** (user's call). **This reverses the 2026-07-27 decision.** Outside the pre-turn window the proposed agent is now bit-for-bit the speaker-following baseline, so the Proposed-vs-B contrast isolates the pattern exactly — measured at 14 differing frames out of 354. The trade is that Proposed-vs-A is no longer a controlled comparison but a comparison of two whole gaze models; **report the pairings accordingly**. Two things fall out of it: the condition has no directional aversion anywhere (B never averts, and the pattern's `None` recentres), which removes the mixed rendering the Baseline A substrate produced; and it is fully deterministic, since B carries no random stream.

- 2026-08-09 — **Each demo take gets one folder, `Recordings/<CaseName>/`, holding the videos *and* their gaze logs.** A video without its log cannot be traced back to the policy state that produced it, and keeping them in separate trees made that separation the default. `LogDirectory` is retired in favour of `OutputDirectory` + `CaseName`.

- 2026-08-02 — **No algorithm-driven body animation: the loaded mocap is used faithfully and gaze is eyes-only** (user's call). `GazeController.HeadContribution` goes to 0, retiring the fractional head turn. It was synthesising motion on top of the clip, and after `TriadConversation` froze the motion players it became the *only* thing moving — ±23° of head swing every half second on a still skeleton, which is the "head shaking" seen at the end of a take. The runner now also stops re-deciding gaze once the conversation has finished, so the tail is a still frame. **This supersedes the 2026-07-30 "HER 0.3 → 0.5" decision**, which came from Shintani 2025's finding that 0.3 reads introverted; report instead that head motion is mocap-only and identical across conditions, so §0.1 still holds.
  - The feared cost did not materialise: the ±35° eye clamp is reached 0 times during the conversation in all three conditions, and only in the frozen 1.5 s tail.

- 2026-08-02 — **Aversion re-targets on Shintani's 0.7 s constant, not the corpus's sampled interval** (user's call, after watching the first takes). This **supersedes the 2026-07-30 decision** to sample the empirical segment distribution. The measured median (0.217 s) produced thirteen direction changes inside one four-second aversion, which reads as darting; the corpus's own unbiased estimator says 0.939 s, and its segments come from an eye tracker at a finer grain than a gaze-shift annotation, so 0.217 s is the doubtful figure and 0.7 s sits inside the corpus's 0.6-0.94 s range. Report as the paper's constant, with our measurement noted.
  - Worth remembering how this was found: the complaint was about the *proposed method's* aversion, but the logs showed the offending episode was the shared Baseline A substrate, and the prototype's own avert segment was 0.28 s. Changing what was asked for would not have changed what was seen.

- 2026-08-02 (later) — **REVERSED: inside its pre-turn window the proposed condition recentres the eyes for `GazeRole.None`** instead of sampling a direction (user's call, asked twice). Outside the window its Baseline A substrate still averts directionally, so the condition renders "looking away" two different ways within a single take, and its aversion no longer matches Baseline A's. This is a known §0.1/§5.3 departure and **must be reported**: it is the one place the conditions differ in how gaze is rendered rather than in what is chosen. `AversionSampler` stays, reached through `ShintaniGazePolicy` only.

- 2026-08-02 — ~~**The proposed condition's aversion uses the same sampler as Baseline A**~~ (`AversionSampler`), not the old "recentre the eyes" rendering of `GazeRole.None` — superseded the same day, see above. The reasoning at the time: sharing the code made §0.1 true by construction rather than by discipline, and the alternative writes zeros into the log's aversion columns for one of the three conditions.

- 2026-08-02 — **The pre-turn pattern fires before every turn end**, not only the scripted A→B hand-over. A policy has no notion of "the interesting turn", and the paper's claim is about turn boundaries in general. Consequence: the demo now shows the prototype twice, including on B's closing turn.

- 2026-08-02 — **The mouth interior is real geometry separated by UV, not a blocker object.** The re-exported SMPL-X FBX carries a mouth bag, but it is unmapped — every one of its vertices sits on UV (0, 0) — so it rendered in whatever colour the agent's albedo happens to hold in its bottom-left texel: dark in the stock atlas, near-white in the SMPLitex one. Splitting those 288 triangles onto their own submesh at import time (`SmplxMouthInteriorSubmesh`) makes the cavity texture-independent, so any future SMPLitex agent gets a correct mouth for free. Chosen over splitting the material in Blender (a round trip per model revision) and over painting the texture corner dark (needs repeating for every new agent texture). The `MouthCavity`/`MouthBackdrop` blockers and their tuning menu are deleted.

- 2026-07-30 — **Baseline A is pure Shintani: no hand-authored turn-boundary overrides, no mutual-gaze breaking** (user's call). `baseline-spec.md` §2 prescribes both, but they belong to the superseded Mutlu/Goffman baseline. The `changing`/`holding` conditioning is the empirically-estimated version of the same effect, and a scripted turn-yielding gaze inside Baseline A would fire in exactly the window the proposed method overrides — contaminating the comparison and, since A is also the proposed method's substrate, both conditions at once. Mutual-gaze breaking is left out as one un-corpus-derived parameter that the measured 0.77-0.88 jump-to-aversion makes unnecessary; it stays checkable because `mutual_gaze_*` is logged.

- 2026-07-30 — **Baseline A's fitted parameters ship as a committed JSON config**, `Assets/GazeControl/Resources/BaselineAParameters.json`, generated by `Tools/build_baseline_a_params.py` from the git-ignored `Research/corpora`. Config over constants is what `baseline-spec.md` §2 asks for, and it means a fresh clone can run the condition without the corpus. The generator is committed so the numbers stay re-derivable.

- 2026-07-30 — **Aversion re-target intervals come from an empirical quantile table, not a fitted law.** Direction segments are clipped by the ends of their aversion, so 17% fall below the corpus's 0.1 s fixation floor while the tail reaches 16.6 s; a lognormal truncated at the floor would inflate the mean interval by about a quarter. The table spans p0-p99 (top 1% = 2.4-16.6 s truncated, and the governing aversion dwell truncates it in practice anyway). Only un-clipped segments are fitted, since the generator clips its own last segment the same way the corpus did.
  - The corpus README's 0.939 s re-targeting estimate (OLS of direction count on aversion duration) is **not** used: sampling intervals from the observed segment distribution reproduces the observed 2.12 directions per aversion by construction, whereas 0.939 s would give 1.8.

- 2026-07-13 — Gaze control and agent motion are both **data-driven**, from gaze behaviour patterns collected before turn-taking in real triad conversations.
- 2026-07-13 — Two target scenes: (1) A↔B turn-taking with the user watching; (2) agent A yields the turn to the user with gaze implication.

RH→LH mirror across the YZ plane: axis `(x,y,z)` → `(x,−y,−z)`, angle kept; positions `(x,y,z)` → `(−x,y,z)`. No up-axis correction needed (data already Y-up; the FBX pelvis parent chain −90°X·+90°X cancels).

- 2026-07-13 — First gaze pattern: **Fig. 8d turn-taking prototype** from the ICMI paper ("current speaker glances at the next speaker twice" in the last second of the turn). Roles map to the demo as A = current speaker, B = next speaker, **user = listener** (camera plays the listener gaze track: steady on the speaker, then to B at the turn). Eyes do most of the gaze (35° clamp), head contributes a 0.3 fraction over the mocap pose.

- 2026-07-30 — **Q3 answered: sampled aversion in every condition**, including the proposed method. `GazeRole.None` stops recentering the eyes and becomes a sampled direction, so the animation layer is identical across conditions (§0.1, §5.3). This visibly changes the signed-off 7e demo — accepted. No guesswork needed: `aversion_direction/` gives 9-way marginals per role, the 9×9 first→second conditional, and **measured az/el per bin** (lateral ≈ ±20° yaw; up bins ≈ +11° pitch, down bins ≈ −13°), which land inside `baseline-spec.md` §1's guessed 15-30° / 10-20° band.
  - Re-targeting cadence: the corpus README claims 0.6-0.94 s "bracketing Shintani's 0.7 s", but `aversion_segments.csv` gives per-segment **median 0.22 s, mean 0.36 s** (2-3 segments per event, ~0.75 s mean aversion). Sample segment durations from the empirical distribution rather than any constant, which sidesteps the conflict.

- 2026-07-30 — **Q4 answered: minimal gaze-direction layer, no blink.** Body motion is pre-defined mocap from file, so the layer's only job is gaze direction. See the task entry for what is kept vs dropped.

- 2026-07-30 — **Corpus event table delivered and validated**, at `Research/corpora/` (git-ignored; regenerate from `F:\Code\scnpro\prototype\prototype`). It answers all three outstanding data questions and changes two plan assumptions:
  - **Use lognormal durations, not χ².** The corpus authors tested both: across role × target × `min_dwell`, **0 of 45 cells** give χ² an interior mode (fitted `dn` 0.88–1.78), and lognormal fits better in 8 of 9 cells (mean KS 0.051 vs 0.070). Shintani's χ² degenerates toward exponential on this data. This lands back on `baseline-spec.md` §2's original log-normal choice. Also: `dloc` is an artifact of the `min_dwell` filter (0.1 s), not a property of gaze.
  - **The "twitchy dwell" worry is resolved.** Real durations are roughly double the geometric ones implied by the transition matrix — mean 0.65–1.11 s, median 0.40–0.58 s, p90 1.3–2.5 s (vs 0.30–0.53 s geometric), with a genuine long tail. Gaze at the *speaker* is longest (~1.1 s), matching Shintani and Mutlu's ~0.98 s.
  - **`ad` is NOT an annotated addressee** — it is `second_speaker`, a hindsight label for whoever actually spoke next, which participants did not have at the time. `first_speaker[k] == second_speaker[k-1]` holds only **47.9%** of the time, so these do not form a floor-passing chain. `sp` is sound; `ad` is loose and `sd` inherits that looseness. Shintani's Addressee is a different variable — say so when reporting.
  - **Aversion direction was recovered** from the raw head-mounted eye tracker (34/38 sessions) rather than annotated: 9-way marginals per role plus the 9×9 first→second conditional. Measured re-targeting period 0.6–0.94 s **brackets Shintani's 0.7 s constant**. Note our distribution is flatter than theirs and lateral-down dominates (ld/rd ≈ 0.15) rather than pure down; `u` is rarest (0.05).
  - Other caveats from the corpus README worth carrying: `changing` covers 57.8% of gazed frames (dense turn annotation — narrow via `frames_to_turn` if needed); 24.26% of fixations outlive their governing event (`spans_events`); censoring is negligible (0.15%, drop it).

- 2026-07-27 — ~~**Baseline A supplies the proposed method's substrate**~~ — **superseded 2026-08-09, the substrate is now Baseline B; see above.** The reasoning at the time: outside the 1 s pre-turn window the proposed agent would *be* a Baseline A agent, isolating the contribution against A. Its consequence — that the transition matrix and dwell distributions sat on the critical path for two of three conditions — no longer holds; only Baseline A reads the corpus model now.

- 2026-07-27 — **Baseline A's parameters come from our own corpus**, not the literature table in `baseline.md` §2 — which is what that spec itself calls "strictly better". Source: `F:\Code\scnpro\prototype\prototype\output\transition_full_conv_legacymap\` (38 sessions, 2.0 M frames @ 60 fps). Two structural findings the literature guess misses: (a) **star topology** — leaving a person, ~90% of jumps go to aversion, not to the other person, so direct person→person shifts are rare; (b) our triad **averts far more** than the published proportions (speaker 0.445 vs 0.40, listener 0.397 vs 0.25, side participant 0.411 vs 0.25) and looks at the speaker much less (0.422 vs 0.65). EoT type (interruption/overlap/turn-taking) is irrelevant — max deviation from pooled is 0.0076, so use pooled.

- 2026-07-27 — The stored matrix is **per-frame at 60 Hz** (diagonals ~0.95), so Baseline A uses the derived **jump chain** (off-diagonals renormalised) plus separate dwell distributions. Reconstructing occupancy as `π·E[dwell]` normalised reproduces the observed occupancy to within 0.004 across all three roles, which validates the semi-Markov formulation — and removes the "solve for a matrix matching the §2 proportions" step from the plan entirely.

- 2026-07-27 — **Baseline B runs on the existing animation layer**; the §4 rewrite is a separate, later task. B uses person-targets only, so the rewrite buys it nothing, and changing `GazeController` would alter the appearance of the signed-off 7e demo unverified.

- 2026-07-27 — **Voice activity is measured from the clip waveform at the playback position**, not `AudioSource.GetOutputData` (which is distance-attenuated, so detection would depend on where the listener stands). When the audio engine's `timeSamples` is not advancing, an internal playback clock takes over — without that fallback a dead output device yields a complete, plausible-looking gaze log in which nobody ever speaks.

- 2026-07-27 — **Condition wiring lives in a menu command** (`GazeControl → Set Up Gaze Conditions`), not in the committed scene, while the scene carries in-flight MouthCavity edits. Note: Unity auto-saved the scene on entering Play Mode during testing, so the wiring had to be reverted by hand afterwards — expect this if you test the same way.

- 2026-07-26 — Agents get distinct appearances via **per-agent materials + SMPLitex SMPL-X textures**. SMPLitex outputs (512², no eyeball UV island) are used as-is for body/face; the eye disc is copied from the default 4096² SMPL-X albedo since both eyes share that single UV island. Agent A stays on the default `SMPLX-Male-URP`.

## Parked / open questions

- **RESOLVED 2026-09-07 — `Separate/..._PC_<N>_...` is mislabelled, and the remap is known.** Its `N` is a position in an **alphabetical list of first names**, not a participant number: the processed CSV stacks its three blocks alphabetically and `csvtotxt-3p.py` slices them positionally, calling block *k* `PC_k`. **Only 5 of the 21 participant-slots across the seven dates are correctly labelled.** Four independent sources agree on the true numbering and disagree with the file names — `Notes.xlsx`'s `PC n (Name)` headers (the user pointed at these), the C3D subject labels in files named `convo<S>_pc<N>`, the `raw_data/pc<N>-<Name>/audio/` folders, and the gaze exports' own first timestamps, which match `Notes.xlsx`'s per-PC `Start (UTC)` to within 4-12 ms on three machines that started ~64 minutes apart. **Gaze, audio and the raw folders carry true PC numbers; only the processed motion does not.** Join on the subject name via `Notes.xlsx`, never on `PC_<N>` across trees. The per-date remap is in `Assets/Docs/3people-motion-sources.md`.
  - **This reaches past our converter.** `Data/main.cpp` reads `Mocap/Separate/..._PC_N_...` alongside `Gaze/Convert/..._PC_N_...` to produce the published `Session_<S>_gazeBehavior.txt` — so on this evidence those annotations pair each participant's motion with a **different** participant's gaze in 16 of the 21 slots. The mechanism is verified from file contents; the pipeline has **not** been re-run to show the annotations change. **A strong claim about someone else's published data — put it to the corpus author before relying on it.** It also undercuts the Euler decision, whose justification was agreeing with those annotations.
  - Pairing a converted clip with a voice is still deferred (motion first), but the blocker is gone: the mapping is known.
